title: How to Co-Facilitate Without Talking Over Each Other
author: Nick Martin
summary: Nick Martin argues that most co-facilitation trouble comes from two experienced facilitators walking in without agreeing how they will share the room, because each brings habits that work alone but collide when doubled. He identifies five problems: talking over each other, one person dominating, messy handoffs, disagreement over direction mid-session, and mismatched energy styles. Each has a fix that can be made at the next break and out of the room’s sight, such as splitting the remaining sections with a "silent unless invited" rule, talking about the split rather than the person, scripting the exact last and first lines of every handoff, never correcting a co-facilitator in front of the group, and assigning energy styles to the parts of the day that suit them. He ends with a worked example of a first-break reset and advises moving the same conversation earlier once it becomes habit. The principle is that the room should only ever see one facilitator leading at a time, and the later sections point to paid templates.
points: Co-facilitation fails because both facilitators bring solo habits like filling silences and adding examples, and the conversation that would prevent the clash feels awkward to start.
Splitting the remaining sections and agreeing "silent unless invited" gives the non-lead a real job of watching faces, time and stuck tables.
Raising imbalance as a problem with the split rather than the person avoids the personal sting of "you’re talking too much."
Scripting only the seams, one agreed last line and first line per handoff, shrinks a handoff to about five seconds without over-scripting the live middle.
Never correct a co-facilitator publicly; let them run it and settle the difference at the break.
quotes: Most of it traces back to the same gap. Two facilitators walked in without agreeing how they’d share the room.
Each of you walks in with the habits that make you good on your own. You fill a silence when it drags. You step in when a group gets stuck.
The one not leading has plenty to do. They watch faces, notice the table that’s stuck, keep an eye on the time and get ready for their own section.
It’s rarely deliberate. Usually it’s nerves, or the more experienced of the two stepping into every gap because they think they’re helping.
Before the session, agree one sentence each for every handoff. Your last line and their first line.
The room reads a public correction between facilitators as one of you deciding the other isn’t up to the job.

Every fix in this piece happens at a break, out of the room’s sight.
